newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia loan should depend on economic need-diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Croatia loan should depend on economic need-diplomats.

text.p: Western diplomats on Tuesday reacted with concern to U.S. suggestions that a $30 million World Bank loan to Croatia could be endangered because of "biased" state television coverage of the country's presidential election campaign.
The loan should be judged on economic criteria alone, diplomats in the Croatian capital said.

Television coverage of the campaign was assessed as biased in favour of President Franjo Tudjman by independent monitors who issued a report on Monday. Tudjman won a second term of office in voting on Sunday,
But diplomats said using the report to sway a decision on much-needed financial assistance would be unjustified.
They said Croatia could not be expected to turn into a flawless democracy overnight after being under communist rule for 50 years and that the election itself was properly conducted.

"This is never going to be the U.S. It's never going to have the same (electoral) tradition as the U.S.," one Western diplomat familiar with Zagreb government policy told Reuters. "I would be indignant if (the report) affected World Bank loans."
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) consulted 104 election observers who monitored the campaign for a month and the voting on Sunday.
It concluded the process leading up to the vote "was marked by serious and substantive deficiencies" and said Croatia had "experienced a free but not fair election".
In its report it highlighted television coverage of each candidate, election funding and other concerns, saying the process "afforded enormous electoral advantages" to Tudjman.
But diplomats and observers said even if the coverage had been fairer, Tudjman would still have won the election.
The editor-in-chief of Croatian Television, Hloverka Novak Srzic, said denied bias towards the president.
"If the election headquarters of the three presidential candidates had come to an agreement on the direct confrontation of the candidates this would most definitely been aired on TV," he said.

Reaction from diplomats in Zagreb came after U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns indicated on Monday Washington may block a $30 million World Bank loan that is expected to be finalised later this month, and referred to the OSCE report.
"Each of these loans is going to be judged on a case-by-case basis" and there has been no decision yet on the $30 million loan, Burns told a news briefing.
But "it doesn't help...when there are so many issues of concern to the OSCE, the objective, independent, international monitor...And I can say that these elections don't help."

One diplomat in Zagreb said that, if the United States were to block loans, "then you have a responsibility for finding other ways of making this society move forward. These things should be judged on economic criteria only."

But veteran U.S. senator Paul Simon, coordinator of the OSCE monitoring mission, told reporters: "You cannot separate the democratic process from economic growth. If the leadership of this country wants to move ahead, be part of Europe, prosper economically, it has to make proper adjustments."
He said Tudjman would probably have been re-elected "regardless of the problems, but perhaps it would have been a closer contest".
One Western envoy said he was worried the OSCE had been influenced by the American position on Croatia.
However, a source close to the OSCE said Simon "was basing his report on 104 observers from at least 25 different countries. So it's not as if he can dictate any national position."
U.S. ambassador to Croatia Peter Galbraith told Reuters Washington did not have an independent reaction. "The American position will correspond closely to the OSCE position," he said.
He said U.S. policy would continue to expect Croatia to adhere to peace agreements and respect the human rights of its Serb minority.
